title: Prioritarianism as a Theory of Value

summaries.example: Imagine two students need help with homework. One student is already doing very well and would gain a small extra advantage. The other is struggling and would gain the same amount of help. Prioritarianism says the help may matter more when it goes to the student who is worse off. It does not simply say that everyone must end up exactly equal.
summaries.summary: Prioritarianism is a theory about which outcomes are morally better. It says that gains and losses affecting people at lower levels of well-being deserve extra weight. For example, helping someone who is struggling can matter more than giving the same help to someone already doing well. A standard version represents each person’s well-being with a number, changes those numbers using an increasing but bending-down function, and adds the results. The bending gives more importance to lower levels. This differs from utilitarianism, which simply adds well-being. Prioritarianism can be connected to consequentialism, the view that choices are right because of their outcomes, but it does not have to be. Philosophers also study whether it should care about equality itself, how it should handle chances and risks, and how it should compare populations of different sizes.
key_ideas: Prioritarianism gives extra moral weight to improvements for people who are worse off.
It differs from utilitarianism, which adds up well-being without giving extra weight based on a person’s starting level.
It is not the same as saying that everyone must have equal well-being.
A common mathematical version adds together transformed well-being scores, using a curve that rises but bends downward.
Philosophers disagree about how prioritarianism should guide choices when outcomes are uncertain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prioritarianism offers one way to think about fairness when making decisions about health, resources, or opportunities. It explains why helping people in greater need might deserve special attention without saying that every difference must be removed. The theory also shows why moral choices can be difficult: giving more weight to the worse off may conflict with treating equal expected benefits alike or with choosing the outcome that is better in every possible situation.

important_terms.definition: A way of thinking about what makes results morally good, bad, better, or worse.
How well a person’s life is going. In this entry, it means well-being over a whole life.
The idea that a benefit or loss matters more when it affects someone who is worse off.
The view that the total amount of well-being matters, without giving extra weight to who receives it.
A possible situation, including how well each person is doing in it.

questions_to_think_about: Should the same-sized benefit matter more when it goes to someone who is worse off?
Is helping the worse off different from making everyone equal?
If one choice has a better possible result in every situation, should it always be chosen?
How should we compare a sure benefit with a risky chance of a larger benefit?

summaries.example: Suppose a treatment can be given to either person A or person B. A would gain 10 well-being units while already at a high level; B would gain the same 10 units while at a much lower level. Utilitarianism counts equal gains equally, so the choice may depend on other gains and losses. Prioritarianism gives B’s gain greater moral weight because the gain occurs at a lower level. This need not mean that equality itself has value, or that B must end up as well off as A.
summaries.summary: Prioritarianism is usually presented as a welfarist moral axiology: among outcomes with the same population, it ranks each outcome by the sum of transformed lifetime well-being. The transformation is strictly increasing, so benefits remain morally positive, and strictly concave, so the same-sized benefit has greater weight at a lower level of well-being. This yields the Pigou-Dalton principle: transferring well-being from a better-off person to a worse-off person, while narrowing the gap and keeping the total fixed, is an improvement. Utilitarianism rejects this preference because the total remains unchanged. Prioritarianism also satisfies separability and continuity; together with standard welfarist assumptions, these distinguish it from several alternatives such as generalized-Gini, leximin, and sufficientist rankings. The entry separates prioritarianism as an outcome ranking from prioritarianism as a justification that gives priority without treating equality as intrinsically valuable. A decomposition result shows that the same ranking can sometimes be represented as total well-being minus an inequality measure, so ranking and justification should not be conflated. Under uncertainty, factualism assesses choices by the outcome that actually occurs, while probabilist views rank prospects using rules such as ex post or ex ante prioritarianism. These approaches face tradeoffs among State Dominance, Expected Utility Decisionmaking, Ex Ante Pareto, and Prospect Separability. The entry also examines utilitarian, egalitarian, and sufficientist challenges, along with problems involving different-sized populations.
key_ideas: The standard fixed-population formulation ranks outcomes by the sum of concavely transformed individual well-being.
Strict increase means that more well-being still contributes positively; strict concavity means that an equal gain has greater moral weight at a lower level.
Pigou-Dalton distinguishes prioritarianism from utilitarianism: equal transfers toward the worse off improve the outcome for prioritarianism but not for utilitarianism.
Separability expresses concern with people’s absolute levels rather than their relative standing compared with unaffected people.
Prioritarianism can be understood as a betterness ranking or, in some debates, as a mode of justification that does not treat equality itself as intrinsically valuable.

Under uncertainty, factualist, ex post, ex ante, and equally distributed equivalent approaches give different guidance, and no standard prioritarian prospect rule satisfies every appealing axiom at once.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory gives a precise framework for the thought that benefits to people in greater need deserve more weight. It is relevant to distributive decisions because it can favor improving the situation of the worse off without requiring strict equality or accepting every form of levelling down. At the same time, its formal commitments create difficult questions about risk, individual claims, thresholds, and future populations. Studying those tensions helps show why a seemingly simple idea—give priority to the worse off—can support several competing theories and decision rules.

important_terms.definition: A theory of moral value that ranks outcomes by what makes them morally good, bad, better, or worse.
The level of how well a person’s life goes; the entry treats it as lifetime well-being and assumes comparisons of levels and differences are possible.
A ranking of outcomes according to moral betterness or worseness.
A family of rankings that sums each person’s well-being after applying a strictly increasing, strictly concave function.
The view that outcomes are ranked by the sum of individual well-being, without extra weight for lower levels.
A principle saying that a transfer from a better-off person to a worse-off person is an improvement when it narrows the gap and leaves the total unchanged.
A condition requiring that unaffected people’s well-being not change the ranking of outcomes that differ only for affected people.
A technical condition requiring rankings to remain stable when well-being levels are changed only by sufficiently small amounts.

questions_to_think_about: Does giving greater weight to lower well-being require caring about equality, or can it be justified without valuing equality itself?
Is it acceptable for prioritarianism to conflict with Ex Ante Pareto, which favors a prospect that is no worse for everyone and better for someone?
Should a moral theory use the actual outcome, expected outcomes, or some other treatment of risk?
Does a threshold above which priority disappears make sense, as sufficientism claims?
How should a prioritarian theory compare outcomes with different numbers of people?

summaries.example: A school has one extra tutoring session. Maya is far behind in algebra; Leo is already near the top of the class. Suppose either student would improve by about the same amount. A utilitarian approach counts the two improvements equally. A prioritarian approach gives Maya’s improvement more weight because it happens at a lower level of achievement. But prioritarianism is not automatically the same as equality: it does not say that Leo must lose anything, or that every student must finish at the same level.
summaries.summary: Prioritarianism is generally understood as a moral axiology: a theory of which outcomes are better or worse. Its central claim is that well-being improvements and losses have greater moral importance when they affect people at lower levels of well-being. In the standard fixed-population model, each person receives a well-being number, a strictly increasing and strictly concave function is applied to each number, and the transformed values are added. Because a concave function rises more slowly at higher levels, a gain to someone worse off can outweigh an equal gain to someone better off. This gives the Pigou-Dalton principle and separates prioritarianism from utilitarianism, which sums untransformed well-being. The entry also identifies separability and continuity as important features. Separability says that the well-being of unaffected people should not change a comparison; continuity rules out abrupt changes in ranking from tiny changes in well-being. These features distinguish standard prioritarianism from other views, including leximin and sufficientism. A further distinction concerns justification. Prioritarianism may describe a ranking, or it may describe a reason for favoring the worse off that does not depend on equality being valuable in itself. Under uncertainty, the theory can be factualist, focusing ultimately on the outcome that occurs, or probabilist, using a rule for comparing prospects. Ex post, ex ante, and equally distributed equivalent rules each preserve some attractive principles while rejecting others. The entry presents challenges from utilitarian, egalitarian, and sufficientist perspectives rather than treating the debate as settled.
key_ideas: Prioritarianism is usually an account of moral value, not by itself a complete theory of which actions are right.
Its standard formula sums transformed well-being. The transformation is increasing and concave, so gains at lower levels receive greater weight.
Utilitarianism and prioritarianism agree that well-being matters, but disagree about whether a person’s level changes the moral weight of a gain.
Prioritarianism differs from egalitarianism because it need not value equality itself or care about how each person compares with others.
The entry distinguishes outcome rankings from ways of justifying those rankings; the same ranking can sometimes be described using total well-being minus an inequality measure.
When choices involve uncertainty, prioritarian theories must choose among competing principles, including actual-outcome assessment, expected value, state dominance, and ex ante fairness.
summaries.why_it_matters: Prioritarianism connects an everyday intuition—helping people in greater need deserves special attention—to a demanding theory of value. It can support concern for the worse off without endorsing strict equality or the idea that making people worse off is good merely because it reduces inequality. Yet the theory must explain how priority operates under uncertainty, whether it should apply in one-person cases, and how it handles thresholds and changing populations. These problems matter whenever institutions compare policies whose benefits and risks fall on different people.

important_terms.definition: A branch of ethics that studies what makes outcomes morally good, bad, better, or worse.
A person’s level of benefit or advantage across their life, treated in the entry as something that can be compared between people.
The claim that improvements for people at lower well-being levels should count more than equal improvements for people at higher levels.
A moral ranking that adds people’s well-being, giving equal-sized gains equal weight regardless of who receives them.
A mathematical function that keeps increasing but increases more slowly as its input rises; this makes lower levels count more heavily.
A principle that favors a balanced transfer from a better-off person to a worse-off person when the transfer narrows their gap and changes no one else.
The view that unaffected people should not alter how two outcomes are compared when only other people are affected.
A theory that gives special priority to people below a chosen level of well-being and changes how priority works above that level.

questions_to_think_about: If a transfer makes one worse-off person slightly better off and another better-off person slightly worse off, why might that be an improvement even when total well-being stays constant?
Could two theories rank outcomes in the same order while giving different reasons for that ranking?
Should a risky prospect be judged by its expected transformed well-being or by the transformed expected well-being of each person?
Is it reasonable to ignore people who are certain to be unaffected by a decision?
Would a threshold for ‘enough’ well-being improve or weaken the case for priority?
